tagline: Forested roads link harbor villages once connected by rail and steamboat.
intro: Forested hills and fields frame the Lake Sunapee Scenic Byway, a 39-mile circuit through Sunapee, Newbury and New London. Lake views arrive as intermittent glimpses and occasional broad openings. Part of New Hampshire’s Scenic and Cultural Byways Program, the route connects harbor villages, The Fells and Mount Sunapee. The byway committee emphasizes those views of water and undeveloped mountainsides as the drive’s distinction.

The villages had once shared a different travel network: rail passengers arriving at Newbury transferred to steamboats for the lake’s villages and grand hotels. Those boats also carried the summer population to Georges Mills and Sunapee Harbor. The byway did not begin as a complete circuit. First designated in the mid-1990s, it included Routes 103 and 103B in Newbury and Sunapee and Route 11 in Sunapee and New London. An extension in 2009 added Route 103A and roads through New London, completing the loop and connecting the three downtown areas.

From New London, travel west on Route 11 through Georges Mills, then south toward Sunapee Harbor. Continue toward Mount Sunapee and Newbury Harbor at the lake’s southern end. Route 103A follows the eastern side north past The Fells and Blodgett Landing toward New London.
notice: Lake views from the car include Georges Mills, Sunapee Harbor, Mount Sunapee State Park Beach and Newbury Harbor.

moments.title: Sunapee Harbor
moments.text: The Sugar River begins its westward journey at Sunapee Harbor, the outlet of Lake Sunapee. The town was an industrial place before tourism took over; one factory produced 110 clothespins a minute. Hames Park, beside the Sugar River on an old factory site, interprets that manufacturing history. Summer visitors also arrived here by steamboat from Newbury’s rail stations. The Sunapee Historical Society Museum occupies the historic Osborne-Flanders Stable. The steamship Kearsarge’s pilothouse was recovered from the lake in the 1960s and is now on display at the Sunapee Historical Center.

moments.title: Newbury Harbor
moments.text: At Lake Station, the journey changed from rails to water. Newbury Harbor’s rail connection fed steamboats that circled Lake Sunapee, carrying passengers to villages and grand hotels. The automobile eventually ended the steamer era. An antique caboose now commemorates the railroad that brought vacationers here. The railroad museum and Center Meeting House interpret that period and its effects on the region. The meetinghouse overlooks the lake’s southern end at the junction of Routes 103 and 103A. Inside the meetinghouse, original box pews face a carved pulpit at the rear of the main chamber.

moments.title: The Fells
moments.text: The main entrance of The Fells’ first cottage faced the lake because the Hay family arrived by boat. The estate was John Hay’s summer home; he served as secretary of state from 1898 until his death in 1905. Architect George Hammond directed its construction in 1891; a guest cottage followed beside it in 1897. After John Hay’s death, his son Clarence and Clarence’s wife Alice transformed the summer cottages. Renovations beginning in 1915 gave the house a Colonial Revival design and turned the connecting breezeway into a formal hall, joining the cottages as one house. A garage was added later as automobile use grew.
